before.title: Total charge, dipole moment, Cartesian moments and traceless quadrupole of a static charge distribution
before.statement:
For the Lebesgue branches (a),(b), assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the exact measure interface ([[def-countable-choice]]). The finite moment sums in branch(c) are defined and computed without Choice. Let the laboratory region, its chart, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\delta_{ij}$ be the Kronecker symbol in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame, with $|y|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This definition assigns **source moments** to a static charge distribution in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d) and (e). Two branches are declared.

(a) [Absolutely continuous branch] Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $\overline B_a(0)=\{y:|y|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The **total charge** $Q$, the **dipole moment** $p$, the **degree-$l$ Cartesian moments** $M_{i_1\dots i_l}$ and the **traceless quadrupole** $Q_{ij}$ are
$$Q:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p_i:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_i\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
$$M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(l\ge0),\qquad Q_{ij}:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl(3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
with $M^{(0)}:=Q$ and $M_i:=p_i$, indices in $\{1,2,3\}$, units C, C m, C m$^l$ and C m$^2$, and integrals in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Each integral is absolutely convergent: since $\rho=0$ $\lambda_3$-a.e. off $\overline B_a(0)$ and the maps $y\mapsto y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}$ and $y\mapsto 3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}$ are bounded there by $a^l$ and $4a^2$, the integrands are dominated $\lambda_3$-a.e. by $a^l|\rho|$ and $4a^2|\rho|$, which lie in $L^1$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). The traceless quadrupole is traceless, $\sum_iQ_{ii}=0$, since $\sum_i(3y_i^2-|y|^2)=0$ pointwise ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]), and replacing $\rho$ by an equal $\lambda_3$-a.e. density changes no moment ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

(b) [General locally integrable branch] If instead $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is real and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^l|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)<\infty$ for a given integer $l\ge0$, then the degree-$l$ Cartesian moments of the same formula are absolutely convergent and defined; if the absolute weighted moment $\int |y|^L|\rho(y)|dy$ is finite for any real $L\ge0$, then every integer Cartesian degree $0\le l\le L$ is defined. The convention $|y|^0=1$ includes the origin. No compact support and no $L^1$-membership is assumed in this branch.

(c) [Finite system of stationary point charges] Let $N\ge0$, $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb R^3$ and $q_1,\dots,q_N\in\mathbb R$ be charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)), read as the stationary point charges $q_k\delta_{x_k}$ in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e). Define
$$Q:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k,\qquad p:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_kx_k,\qquad M_{i_1\dots i_l}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\,x_{k,i_1}\cdots x_{k,i_l},\qquad Q_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^Nq_k\bigl(3x_{k,i}x_{k,j}-|x_k|^2\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$
finite sums in the sense of [[def-finite-sum]] ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]); again $\sum_iQ_{ii}=0$. The points need not be distinct; charges at a common point add.

(d) [Reference point and scope] Every moment is computed about the chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; this origin is part of the definition. These are source moments of a prescribed static distribution — not momenta, rest masses, intrinsic spins, self-energies or dynamical quantities — and no field, force, equation of motion, equilibrium or empirical claim is made here; the static regime in which the source is read is the adopted idealisation of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (f). Every Cartesian degree l in this definition is a nonnegative integer (the number of Cartesian indices); only the absolute weighted exponent L in(b) may be any nonnegative real number.
before.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition with its well-definedness checks displayed in the clauses: absolute convergence and null-set irrelevance in (a), the finite-absolute-moment hypothesis in (b), and the finite-sum identities in (c). The mathematical inputs are the Lebesgue interface ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]), the pointwise bounds $|y_{i_1}\cdots y_{i_l}|\le a^l$ and $|3y_iy_j-|y|^2\delta_{ij}|\le4a^2$ on $\overline B_a(0)$, the triangle and monotonicity estimates ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]), linearity of the integral ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]), null-set irrelevance ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]) and finite-sum algebra ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]). The physical reading uses only the fixed-time dictionary of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (d), (e); no Choice beyond the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the measure interface is used. For branch (b), local integrability on the compact closed unit ball gives $\int_{|y|\le1}|\rho|<\infty$. For a real $L\ge0$ and integer $0\le l\le L$, on that ball $|y|^l\le1$, while on $|y|>1$ one has $|y|^l\le|y|^L$. Split the nonnegative integral into these two measurable sets and use [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le\int_{|y|\le1}|\rho|+\int_{|y|>1}|y|^L|\rho|<\infty$. Cartesian monomials of degree l have modulus at most |y|^l, so all lower moments exist, including Q at l0. Thus L1 follows as a consequence, not as an added hypothesis. The finite-point algebra in (c) is choice-free independent of the Lebesgue branches. The unit-ball split uses numerical coordinates in the fixed SI chart. Equivalently for any chosen radius Rstar>0 one obtains the dimensionally explicit bound $\int|y|^l|\rho|\le R_\ast^l\int_{|y|\le R_\ast}|\rho|+R_\ast^{l-L}\int_{|y|>R_\ast}|y|^L|\rho|$, with Rstar set to the coordinate unit radius in the preceding proof.

references.locator: Section 2.2.3 printed pp. 20-22 (Q = integral rho, p = integral r' rho, and the symmetric traceless quadrupole Q_ij = integral rho (3 r'_i r'_j - delta_ij r'^2)). Read in the stamped full text.

references.locator: Sections 40-41 printed pp. 95-100 (dipole moment d = sum e_a r_a, Eq. (40.3) p. 95, and quadrupole moment D_ab = sum e (3 x_a x_b - r^2 delta_ab), Eq. (41.3) p. 98; Gaussian units re-expressed in SI). Read in the stamped full text.

before.physical_scope: Source moments (total charge, dipole moment, Cartesian moments, traceless quadrupole) of a prescribed static charge distribution read at fixed time in one named inertial frame: an absolutely continuous compactly supported $L^1$ density, a locally integrable density with a finite absolute moment of the stated order, or a finite system of stationary point charges. These are kinematic source characteristics: no field, force, dynamics, self-energy, stability or empirical content is asserted, and the static regime is an adopted idealisation. In the noncompact locally integrable branch a finite weighted absolute moment may have any real exponent L>=0 and supplies every integer Cartesian degree<=L by the local unit-ball and outer weighted estimate; L1 is a conclusion, not an added hypothesis. Finite moment-sum algebra is choice-free.

before.title: The electric and magnetic fields as fixed-time spatial vector fields
before.statement: Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An electric field of class $C^k$ on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a magnetic field of class $C^k$ is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses: $C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and no regularity beyond it is asserted. Conventions: (a) $E$ is a polar vector and $B$ an axial vector relative to the orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] are proper and orientation preserving, so orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them; (b) the fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at a point of singular source support is asserted; (c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T; (d) the identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] and is not presupposed here.
before.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: the fields are maps on the product $\Omega\times I$ of the laboratory region with a stated class of regularity, and their fixed-time readings are spatial vector fields in the frame basis. The regularity notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the polar/axial convention and the exclusion of pointwise values at singular source support are conventions recorded explicitly rather than used implicitly. No differential equation and no derived quantity is introduced by this definition.

before.title: Laboratory geometry: a restricted inertial chart, its spatial slices and fixed-time fields
before.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

before.reference: definition-contracts.md#def-em-gauge-transformation and definition-contracts.md#def-em-retarded-point-geometry (locally constructed mathematical vocabulary; recorded in the batch notes)
before.design_state: complete-exact-definition-from-literature-conventions; added by this scaffolder as a necessary prerequisite for lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability and lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields
before.statement:
Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$ (for an integer $k\ge0$) is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega	o\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] (the components of $A$ componentwise). For such a pair with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are $$E(\varphi,A):=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ where $
abla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\operatorname{div}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega	o\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function $$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$ also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$. For $k\ge2$ and a $C^k$ function $\chi:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ (a **gauge function**) the **gauge transform** of the pair is $$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+
abla\chi),$$ again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$. Finally, for a $C^2$ function $u:\Omega	o\mathbb R$ put $$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$ with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a $C^2$ map $U:\Omega	o\mathbb R^m$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise. Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+
abla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$ and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.
before.strategy: Vocabulary and regularity audit; a definition asserts no existence theorem. (i) If $\varphi,A$ are $C^k$ then $\nabla\varphi$ and the three partial derivatives $\partial_tA_i$ are $C^{k-1}$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), so $E(\varphi,A)$ is a $C^{k-1}$ map $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ and likewise $B(\varphi,A)$ and $G(\varphi,A)$ for $k\ge1$, since the curl and divergence of a $C^1$ field are computed pointwise from first partial derivatives ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). (ii) For a $C^k$ gauge function with $k\ge2$, $\partial_t\chi$ and $\nabla\chi$ are $C^{k-1}$, so $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a pair of class $C^{k-1}$. (iii) The wave expression is the stated normalization: [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] fixes $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$, so $c^{-2}\Box_c=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta=W$, and $\Delta$ is the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (iv) No solvability is asserted: existence of $\chi$ with $W\chi=G$ is supplied later on this page under slab hypotheses, and it carries the Axiom of Countable Choice through the cited wave theorem. The definition is stated on an arbitrary open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ so that both the full slab and complements of worldlines are instances.

before.title: Worldlines, four-velocity, chart readings and the frame/observer distinction
before.statement: The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Worldlines] A worldline is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A massive worldline is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere nonzero future timelike tangent; a light ray is a $C^1$ future null curve with everywhere nonzero future null tangent. A null curve has zero proper-time increment along every subinterval and no proper-time parametrization ([[def-sr-proper-time]]), and it is never treated as a massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$ in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of another observer. (b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. (c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline has laboratory reading $t\mapsto r(t)$ in a chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity $U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor $\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. (d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. An observer congruence and a noninertial tetrad field are further objects, not defined by this item; the words 'frame', 'chart', 'observer' and 'tetrad' denote distinct notions and are not interchangeable. (e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or polarisation structure in this definition.
before.strategy: A definition reusing the special-relativity curve notions with their exact statements rather than restating them: regularity and causal character of curves are those of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]; proper time and its non-applicability to null curves are those of [[def-sr-proper-time]]; $U$ and $A$ are those of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; the identities $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, $\eta(U,A)=0$, the chart bound $|r'|<c$ and the velocity reading $U=\gamma(c,r')$ are the exact clauses of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. The frame/observer distinction is the one of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] together with the rest-space and projection clauses of the same theorem. The item adds the physical interpretation adopted in [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and records the scope exclusions; it proves no dynamical statement.

before.title: Uniformly subluminal prescribed worldline, retarded root and retarded geometric data off the worldline
before.statement: Let the laboratory region, inertial chart, spatial Euclidean structure and SI units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], in particular $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. A **retarded point-geometry datum** consists of a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs ([[def-em-sources]](a)) and a prescribed map $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) together with a constant $0\le v_*<c$ such that $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the spacetime curve $s\mapsto(z(s),s)$ is the laboratory reading of a prescribed massive future timelike worldline of the physical model ([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]]), and $v_*$ is a declared bound on its coordinate speed, not a measured quantity. Write $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$ and $D:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:x\ne z(t)\}$ for the open off-worldline observation domain. Then: (a) [Retarded root] For every observation event $(x,t)\in D$ there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$; the map $s:D\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with the data of (b) below one has $\partial_ts=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$ ([[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], whose $C^3$ branch applies because $z$ is $C^3$ and uniformly subluminal). (b) [Retarded data] For $(x,t)\in D$ define $R:=x-z(s(x,t))$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s(x,t))/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s(x,t))/c$; then $r=c(t-s)$ and $\kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c]\subseteq(0,\infty)$. On $D$ the objects $r$ and $n$ are of class $C^3$, $\beta$ and $\kappa$ are of class $C^2$, and $\dot\beta$ is of class $C^1$ (each is a composition of the $C^3$ root with $z$ or its derivatives). (c) [Emission-event data and emitted spheres] At an emission event $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a direction $n\in S^2$ put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$, $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in D$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$: the sphere $\{x_r\}$ at observation time $t_r$ is emitted at the single event $s_0$. (d) [Branches and scope] Only the all-time uniformly subluminal branch (a)-(c) is defined by this datum. For a curve prescribed on a finite interval $J$ the same formulas define retarded data only at observation events for which the root equation has a solution $s\in J$; each consumer must assume that cone intersection explicitly. Pointwise subluminality $|z'(s)|<c$ for every finite $s$ does not imply (a): the companion example on the examples page exhibits a smooth curve with $|z'|<c$ pointwise for which the retarded equation has no root at some event, so the uniform bound $v_*<c$, or an explicit cone-intersection hypothesis, is part of the datum. This definition is kinematic: it fixes the root, the retarded data and the notation, and asserts no field, no dynamics, no force law, no self-force and no empirical content. The identification of these data with the emission data of the physical field is made by the selection postulate [[post-em-radiation-selection]] together with the theorems of this page.
before.strategy: An explicit definition with its well-definedness discharged by a cited mathematical supplier. Existence, uniqueness and $C^3$ regularity of $s$ on $D$, together with $\kappa\in[1-v_*/c,1+v_*/c]$ and the derivative formulas, are exactly the all-time uniformly subluminal $C^3$ branch of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] (its statement covers every event of $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, hence every off-worldline event, and identifies equality $s=t$ with $x=z(t)$); no new analysis is needed, and the phrase 'prescribed worldline' is licensed by [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]](a),(c), which relates chart readings $t\mapsto r(t)$ of massive worldlines to the condition $|r'(t)|<c$. Clause (c) is the elementary root check $t_r-s_0=|x_r-z(s_0)|/c=r/c$ combined with the uniqueness in (a); no boundedness of $z''$ is used. Clause (d) records the branch boundaries honestly: the finite-history and nonuniform cases are left to consumers, and the failure of existence under mere pointwise subluminality is not asserted here but exhibited on the examples page. The definition introduces no physical field, so no Maxwell, self-force or empirical assertion is made; the cross-reference to the selection postulate records that the retarded root is the kinematic object that the adopted selection turns into an emission time. No choice principle beyond that carried by the cited root lemma is used.
before.physical_scope: Kinematic definition of the retarded emission data of a prescribed uniformly subluminal $C^3$ worldline in the framework's laboratory chart: retarded root, distance, direction, speed ratio and emission-time Jacobian off the worldline, and the emitted-sphere family. Excluded: any field, Maxwell equation, dynamics, force law, self-force, radiation reaction, existence under a merely pointwise subluminal or finite-history curve, and every empirical or measurement claim.

before.title: Framework-local SI units, the vacuum constants and the exact/measured status of their values
before.statement: Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted (the pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate/uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value); the electric constant is defined within the framework by $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of [[def-em-sources]] carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ carries kg m s$^{-1}$ ([[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]); field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI, they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]].
before.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalisation $x^0=ct$, the unit of each quantity used in this framework, the exact SI defining values of $c$ and $e$ and the measured status of $\mu_0$. The exact values $c=299\,792\,458$ m/s and $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and the statements that the new definition of the ampere fixes $e$ rather than $\mu_0$, that $\mu_0$ must now be determined experimentally, and that $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$ remains exact, are taken from the SI brochure's defining-constants table and its ampere section. The framework's definition of $\varepsilon_0$ by $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ is a definition consistent with that exact relation; the uncertainty carried by $\varepsilon_0$ is recorded rather than hidden. The dimensional checks of the framework's equations and couplings are developed on the companion examples page of this pair. No exact or current measured numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted and no experiment is claimed. The historical nominal and adoption uncertainty are explicitly source context, not a substitution for the current experimentally determined constant.

before.title: Charge parameter, frame charge and current densities, volume charge and flux, and the four-current
before.statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is not asserted. (b) [Smooth source fields] A smooth (volume) source field on $\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the frame charge density (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the frame current density (A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if $V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define $Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$ by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf1_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$
where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is defined through its positive and negative parts ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). This integral is absolutely finite, since $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on $\overline V$ and $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure. On the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption, $Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]. The empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal field $n_S$ the current flux at time $t$ is $\int_S J(y,t)\cdot n_S(y)\,dS$ ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them. (c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and $j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model, and hence the component transformation law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts. This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents. (d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch] Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a $C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier $\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so $u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic convention is $j^0=c\rho$,
$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$
Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$, including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike $U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is $v^i:=cu^i$.
For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch, $U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and
$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$
Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model: in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$ (equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are retained. (e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.
before.strategy:
Keep clauses (a)-(c) as explicit source types and the adopted physical identification. The compact Jordan branch uses [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]] and [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]; flux uses [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. For the broader Lebesgue branch assume the explicitly stated Countable Choice, without Dependent Choice or a convergence/FTC assumption. Fix $t$ and an admitted nonempty $V$. The continuous function $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded by $M_t<\infty$ in absolute value on compact $\overline V$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]. Its zero extension $F_t$ is Borel: for every open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$, the inverse image inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively open and hence open in $\mathbb R^3$; add the closed complement of $\Omega$ precisely when $0\in O$. This is also the open-set form of [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]. Under Countable Choice, Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]) and bounded measurable $V$ has finite measure ([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]). Positive/negative parts and their restrictions by $\mathbf1_V$ are measurable by [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. The bound $|F_t|\mathbf1_V\le M_t\mathbf1_V$ and [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] give
$$\int|F_t|\mathbf1_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty,$$
where the indicator integral is its simple-function value by [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]. This proves exactly the absolute signed integrability required by [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and defines $Q$ using the nonnegative restrictions of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]. For empty $V$ the product is zero. On compact Jordan $V$, the continuous density restricted to V has a bounded Borel zero extension to a bounding rectangle, so the exact compact-Jordan clause of [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], also under Countable Choice, identifies the two finite integral values. The algebraic supplier [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]](vii) gives $j=\rho_0U=\rho_0U^0u$; its coordinate density is $j^0$, whereas the present SI source convention defines $j^0=c\rho$. Division by $c>0$ gives $\rho=\rho_0U^0/c$ and $\rho-\rho_0=\rho_0(U^0-c)/c$, proving exactly the stated equality cases. The spatial components give $J^i=c\rho u^i$. Neither $U^0=c$ nor chart normalization $u^0=1$ is a proper-four-velocity condition.
In the additional normalized material model, write $v=c(U^1,U^2,U^3)/U^0$. The norm equation $-(U^0)^2+|U_{\mathrm{sp}}|^2=-c^2$ gives $(U^0)^2(1-|v|^2/c^2)=c^2$, and future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$ and $|v|<c$, so $U^0=c\gamma$. This is the exact four-velocity/relative-velocity content of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]; substitution gives $\rho=\gamma\rho_0$ and $J=\rho v$. In its comoving frame $U^0=c$, hence the source convention identifies the scalar multiplier with the stipulated rest-frame density. Since $\gamma=1$ if and only if $v=0$, the normalized equality cases follow, including $\rho_0=0$. All density readings remain within the adopted current model; no conservation, measurement, general current factorization, force law or singular-source regularity is deduced.

before.title: Vacuum electromagnetic energy density and energy flux (the Poynting vector)
before.statement:
Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its SI conventions be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$. Define the **electromagnetic energy density** $u$ and the **energy flux density** (Poynting vector) $S$ by
$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0\lvert E(x,t)\rvert^2}{2}+\frac{\lvert B(x,t)\rvert^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t),$$
where $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$ uses the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame basis, and $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ is the constant of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Then $u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] (they are polynomials in the components of $E,B$), with $u$ in $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ in $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$; at fixed $t\in I$, $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued function and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ a spatial vector field on $\Omega$, read in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.
(a) [Pointwise definition] The definitions use only the values of $E,B$ at the same point $(x,t)$; no derivative of the fields and no convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame is used. (b) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable and no product of distributions is defined: the displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$ pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated, is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of singular source support. (c) [Quadratic character] $u$ and $S$ are quadratic in the fields, so decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms generally contribute. (d) [Status] This item defines quantities only; the interpretation of $u$ and $S$ as an energy density and an energy flux is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]], and no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a covariant tensor is made here.
before.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition. The domain and regularity are those of [[def-em-fields]] with the class notion of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the units and the relation $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the inner and cross products are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. The claim that $u$ and $S$ are again of class $C^k$ is the sum/product/composition calculus of [[thm-chain-sum-product-and-composition-rules-for-banach-derivatives]] read componentwise. Exclusions (b) and (c) are recorded in the item, not left tacit: no distributional product is defined, no value is assigned at singular source support, and quadratic expressions are not additive. No field equation, derivative of the fields, or physical interpretation is introduced by this definition.

before.title: Distributional Maxwell equations with point and stationary-sheet sources
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]] ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing $\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the distributional partial derivatives are $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on $U$ are identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$ (coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],
$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$
define distributions on $U$ with $\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead $I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with
$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$
([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let $\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current density; the sheet is stationary). Then
$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$
define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the functionals are bounded by $(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional hypotheses of interface/jump results, not admission requirements of the general weak model.
For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$ are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighborhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial/temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders.
For the broader weak-trace branch, one may instead assume the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ for $dSdt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$ traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade. Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen normal convention. (e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable volume densities with the charge/current quantity types of [[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b) or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings
$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$
all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c). This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here; adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or $J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for these sources is proved separately where used), and no regularisation. Sources that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources, moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are outside the definition.
before.strategy: An explicit definition-contract item. Clause (a) is the regular-distribution identification. Clause (b) restates the pairings and the continuity theorem of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] with its properness hypothesis, and its finite-endpoint variant with the two endpoint deltas. Clause (c) defines the stationary-sheet pairings by explicit iterated integrals; well-definedness uses the finiteness of the surface measure of the compact $S$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[def-em-surface-distribution]]), continuity of $\sigma,K,\psi$ on compact sets and compactness of the time projection of the support of a test function, so both functionals are continuous of finite order on each test-support space. Clause (d) retains the unrestricted locally integrable field pair for the weak predicate, including sheet sources. It records optional interface hypotheses separately: joint one-sided spacetime C1 extensions support the pointwise branch; the weaker per-time spatial C1 trace branch needs the explicit piecewise-derivative and sheet-trace L1 hypotheses for its distribution/a.e. conclusions. Neither branch is a general weak-field admission condition, and separate spatial C1 traces alone are not claimed to give joint continuity or temporal bounds. Clause (e) defines the weak equations by the four vanishing pairings, with distributional derivatives of the regular distributions of the fields; the singular source terms enter only as the explicitly defined functionals of (b) and (c), never as products with the fields. Clause (f) records the exclusions; in particular the product of a singular source density with a field, which would be an undefined product of distributions, is not part of the definition. The vanishing-pairing clause is a precise mathematical solution predicate. It agrees with the old postulate on its original locally integrable source class, but does not extend that physical postulate deductively to singular sources; physical adoption is a separate postulate. It remains possible for a declared source pair to be incompatible with those equations, and no existence is asserted.

before.title: Every smooth potential pair on a slab can be put in Lorenz gauge by a wave-equation gauge function, without changing the fields
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), carried through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its sphere integrations ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0<T$, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ on the slab $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: $\varphi$ and $A$ are restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Put $G:=G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then: (a) there is a gauge function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (b) the gauge-transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\,A+\nabla\chi)$ is again of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and its fields are unchanged: $$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }Q;$$ (c) the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge: $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (d) if $\chi_1,\chi_2$ are of class $C^2$ on $Q$ in the extension sense and $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, then $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$. Nothing is asserted about prescribed boundary values of $\chi$ on a bounded spatial domain, about spatial decay of $\chi$, or about Lorenz gauge fixing for a cavity problem with prescribed boundary data; the older global gauge promise on bounded domains is outside this result.

used_after.title: Every smooth potential pair on a slab can be put in Lorenz gauge by a wave-equation gauge function, without changing the fields
used_after.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), carried through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its sphere integrations ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0<T$, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ on the slab $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: $\varphi$ and $A$ are restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Put $G:=G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then: (a) there is a gauge function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (b) the gauge-transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\,A+\nabla\chi)$ is again of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and its fields are unchanged: $$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }Q;$$ (c) the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge: $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; (d) if $\chi_1,\chi_2$ are of class $C^2$ on $Q$ in the extension sense and $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, then $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$. Nothing is asserted about prescribed boundary values of $\chi$ on a bounded spatial domain, about spatial decay of $\chi$, or about Lorenz gauge fixing for a cavity problem with prescribed boundary data; the older global gauge promise on bounded domains is outside this result.

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos lecture notes (2026 printing)
references.locator: §6.1, printed pp. 134-135: the gauge transformation $A^\mu\to A^\mu+\partial^\mu\chi$, the claim that the Lorenz condition $\partial_\mu A^\mu=0$ can always be arranged by a gauge function solving $\Box\chi=f$, with the reduction $\partial_\mu A'^\mu=\partial_\mu A^\mu+\Box\chi$ and its use in (6.4)

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Partial Differential Equations: From Classical to Modern (2025 archived author manuscript, AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics)
references.locator: §7.1, printed pp. 167-170, Corollary 7.3 and (7.11)-(7.12): existence and smoothness of the solution of $u_{tt}=c^2\Delta u+f$ with prescribed Cauchy data on a slab, the supplier of the gauge function $\chi$ via $W\chi=G$

before.title: Global existence, uniqueness and differentiability of the retarded root
before.statement: Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.
before.strategy: The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\ge s$, $s\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\epsilon\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction.

before.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
before.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, let $a<b$, and let $f$ and $\partial_tf$ be continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, with relative derivatives at the endpoints, and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$. The same conclusion holds, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], with surface measure on a fixed compact $C^1$ hypersurface in place of $K$ and Lebesgue measure. Nothing is asserted for moving parameter sets or for singularities crossing $K$.
before.strategy: For fixed $x$ the mean value theorem writes $[f(x,t+h)-f(x,t)]/h=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$ for some $\tau$ between $t$ and $t+h$; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact product bounds the integral of the difference by the sup-error times the finite measure. Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

before.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
before.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
before.strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

before.title: Retarded Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields of a uniformly subluminal smooth point source
before.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
before.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as stipulated in the statement. (a) Apply [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] to the $C^1$ curve $z$ on $\mathbb R$; $C^3$ is a special case, and its all-time graph is proper because a compact ambient set bounds the time coordinate.
(b) Fix a compact observation set $Q\subseteq\{(x,t):|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$, and tests supported in $Q$. If $g(s,y):=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c)\in Q$, then $s\le t_1$. For $s\le0$, using $|z(s)|\le Z+v_*|s|$ with $Z:=|z(0)|$ gives
$$t_0\le s+|y|/c=s+|x-z(s)|/c\le -(1-v_*/c)|s|+(M+Z)/c.$$
Thus $s\ge-S$, where $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$. If $[-S,t_1]$ is empty no contributing point exists. Otherwise set $H:=\max(S,|t_1|)$ and $L:=1+M+Z+v_*H$. Every contributing $y$ has $|y|\le M+|z(s)|<L$. Consequently the pulled-back support lies in the bounded closed cylinder $[-S,t_1]\times\overline B_L$, possibly approaching $y=0$; it need not be compact inside $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$.
On that cylinder, $|\psi(g(s,y))|/(4\pi|y|)\le\|\psi\|_\infty/(4\pi|y|)$. The polar formula [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives $\int_{B_L}|y|^{-1}dy=\sigma(S^2)L^2/2<\infty$. Borel product identification [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]] and the Euclidean/product-measure bridge [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] allow [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] for the absolute value. Then [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] identifies the double integral with the explicit iterated history integral. In particular, with $T:=\max(0,t_1+S)$ and $M_Q:=T\sigma(S^2)L^2/(8\pi)$,
$$|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|\le |q|M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty/\varepsilon_0,\qquad
|\langle\Upsilon_j,\psi\rangle|\le\mu_0|q|v_*M_Q\|\psi\|_\infty.$$
The seminorm $\psi\mapsto|\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle|$ restricts continuously to each fixed-support test space by these bounds, and likewise for each component of $\Upsilon$. Thus [[def-test-function-topology]] and [[def-distribution]] prove distribution continuity directly; no action of $\rho$ or $J$ on a noncompact test is assumed.
The graph $\Gamma$ is closed: convergence of $(z(s_j),s_j)$ forces $s_j\to t$ and $z(s_j)\to z(t)$. Thus $V:=\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ is open. On $U$, $g$ is $C^1$, and in coordinate order $(s,y_1,y_2,y_3)$ its determinant is $-\kappa(s,y)$, with $\kappa=1-(y/|y|)\cdot z'(s)/c\ge1-v_*/c>0$. If $g(s,y)=g(s',y')$, then $|s-s'|=||y'|-|y||/c\le|z(s')-z(s)|/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, so $s=s'$ and $y=y'$. No image point belongs to $\Gamma$: otherwise $|y|=|z(t)-z(s)|\le v_*(t-s)=v_*|y|/c$, contradicting $y\ne0$. Conversely every point of $V$ has the unique retarded root supplied by [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], giving inverse $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$. Its $C^1$ regularity follows from that supplier's $C^3$ branch on the open domain $x\ne z(t)$, using this consumer's $C^3$ hypothesis. No exclusion of the entire spatial trajectory is imposed. Therefore $g:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism.
For any compact $Q\subseteq\Omega$, the nonnegative Borel substitution lemma [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]] applied to $1_Q/(\kappa r)$ on $V$ yields
$$\int_V\frac{1_Q}{\kappa r}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\frac{1_Q(g(s,y))}{|y|}\,ds\,dy<\infty.$$
The same bound holds for $|\beta|/(c\kappa r)$ since $|\beta|\le v_*/c$. Extend the potentials by zero on the closed graph. These extensions are Borel and locally integrable on all of $\Omega$. Applying the same Borel substitution first to the absolute value of $\psi/(\kappa r)$ establishes its $L^1$ integrability on $V$, and [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]] then gives the scalar pairing formula in the statement. Apply it componentwise to $z'(s)$-weighted data for the vector formula. Its prefactor is
$$\frac{\mu_0qz'(s)}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0qc\beta}{4\pi\kappa r}=\frac{\mu_0c\varepsilon_0 C\beta}{\kappa r}=\frac{C\beta}{c\kappa r},$$
since $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$. The regular-distribution identities mean the zero extensions, as in [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]; tests may be nonzero on $\Gamma$. The retarded root is $C^3$ on $V$, and $r,n$ are $C^3$ while $\beta,\kappa,D$ are $C^2$ with $D>0$, so the potentials are $C^2$. The same composition argument gives the matching $C^k$ and $C^\infty$ branches.

used_after.title: Retarded Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields of a uniformly subluminal smooth point source
used_after.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq\Omega$. For $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ let $s=s(x,t)$ be the unique retarded root of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]] with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and put $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $N:=n\cdot\beta$, $D:=\kappa r$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ and $d:=n\cdot\dot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: (a) the distributions $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\,\psi(z(s),s)\,ds,$$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. (b) Let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and, for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and $\tau\in\mathbb R$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$, put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$. Define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals
$$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds,\qquad
\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds.$$
Here the second integral is componentwise. The notation $\varepsilon_0^{-1}\langle\rho,K\circledast\psi\rangle$ and $\mu_0\langle J,K\circledast\psi\rangle$, if used, means precisely these explicit history integrals, rather than ordinary distribution action on a compactly supported test. These pairings define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta(x,t)}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi(x,t)}{\kappa(x,t)\,r(x,t)}\,dx\,dt$$ (for $\Upsilon$, componentwise against $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; both integrands are continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and integrable there against $\psi$). Consequently the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $$\varphi:=\frac{C}{D}=\frac{C}{\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R,\qquad A:=\frac{\beta\,\varphi}{c}=\frac{\beta\,C}{c\,\kappa r}:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R^3$$ off the worldline, and the zero extensions $\widetilde\varphi,\widetilde A$ on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; $\Phi$ is the regular distribution of $\widetilde\varphi$, and $\Upsilon$ that of $\widetilde A$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function|regular distribution]]). (c) Let $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]). Then, off the worldline, $$E=C\left[\frac{(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r}\right],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}.$$ The fields $E,B$ are $C^1$ off the worldline. More generally, if $z\in C^k$, $k\ge3$, the retarded root is $C^k$, the potentials are $C^{k-1}$ and the fields are $C^{k-2}$ there; if $z\in C^\infty$, all these objects are smooth off the worldline. The result is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated uniformly subluminal smooth worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved.
