before.title: Divergence of the point-charge field energy and the limits of mass inference
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue and polar interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $q\in\mathbb R$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $E_q$ be the ideal point-charge field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d) ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]). For $0<\delta<R$ put
$$U_q(\delta,R):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}}|E_q(x)|^2\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
(the truncated field energy of the shell between the two spheres, [[def-metric-ball]]). Then:
(a) [Exact truncated energy] for all $0<\delta<R$,
$$U_q(\delta,R)=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr);$$
(b) [Divergence] $\lim_{R\to\infty}U_q(\delta,R)=q^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$, and for $q\ne0$
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}U_q(\delta,R)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }R>0;$$
so the field energy of the ideal point charge is locally infinite at its own location, and any finite-energy treatment of a point-like charge must modify the source/field near the singularity or introduce an explicit cutoff;
(c) [Limits of the mass inference] the identity is a divergence of the *field energy of the idealised point source* in the framework's SI conventions. It does not assert that a physical particle has infinite rest mass, does not identify field energy with rest mass, contains no measurement, and involves neither a self-force nor a contradiction claim for classical electrodynamics: the framework supplies no mass-energy identification for a charged particle, and the smooth compact-source field/assembly energy of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] remains finite. The compact $L^1$ branch of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] retains its locally integrable potential and distributional Poisson equation; it does not guarantee finite field energy for arbitrary $L^1$ densities. The point source itself is the idealisation of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); its energy divergence is a mathematical property of that idealisation, not an empirical result.
before.strategy:
For (a), $|E_q(x)|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^2)$ for $x\ne x_0$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]), so $|E_q|^2=q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2|x-x_0|^4)$ and by the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] with the unit-sphere measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]] and [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]; the integrand is nonnegative and Borel, [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]])
$$\int_{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R}|E_q|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot 4\pi\int_\delta^R r^{-2}\,dr=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr),$$
where the one-dimensional integral is evaluated by the fundamental theorem and the derivative of $r\mapsto-1/r$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]); multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ gives (a) ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). For (b), let $R\to\infty$ in (a) for fixed $\delta$ (the left-hand integral increases to the exterior integral by monotone convergence, [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], giving the first limit) and let $\delta\downarrow0$ for fixed $R$: $1/\delta\to\infty$ for $q\ne0$ (directly from the explicit formula and the order properties of the reals), so the truncated energies tend to $+\infty$. Any neighbourhood of $x_0$ therefore contains field energy exceeding any prescribed bound. For (c): the computation uses only the idealised point-source field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d); it makes no use of, and does not assert, a mass-energy relation for a charged particle, a self-force, a regularisation or any measurement ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]); the contrast with the finite energies of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] is the contrast between an extended compactly supported source and the point idealisation. No claims about the field at $x_0$ itself are made: the truncated integrals avoid the singularity ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]). The choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the Lebesgue/polar interface. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.

The point source itself is the idealisation of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); its energy divergence is a mathematical property of that idealisation, not an empirical result.
used_after.strategy:
For (a), $|E_q(x)|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^2)$ for $x\ne x_0$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d), [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]), so $|E_q|^2=q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2|x-x_0|^4)$ and by the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] with the unit-sphere measure of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]] and [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]; the integrand is nonnegative and Borel, [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]])
$$\int_{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R}|E_q|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot 4\pi\int_\delta^R r^{-2}\,dr=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr),$$
where the one-dimensional integral is evaluated by the fundamental theorem and the derivative of $r\mapsto-1/r$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]); multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ gives (a) ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). For (b), let $R\to\infty$ in (a) for fixed $\delta$ (the left-hand integral increases to the exterior integral by monotone convergence, [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], giving the first limit) and let $\delta\downarrow0$ for fixed $R$: $1/\delta\to\infty$ for $q\ne0$ (directly from the explicit formula and the order properties of the reals), so the truncated energies tend to $+\infty$. No claims about the field at $x_0$ itself are made: the truncated integrals avoid the singularity ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]). The choice cost is the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the Lebesgue/polar interface. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.

before.title: Local and fixed-volume electromagnetic energy balance
before.statement:
Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the jointly $C^1$ fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]] (so the additional derivatives required by each displayed Maxwell equation exist and are continuous), the continuous source fields $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]], the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and the energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]].
(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$,
$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E,$$
where $\operatorname{div}$ is the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$ and $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].
(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the hypothesis under which that divergence theorem is stated. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$
(c) [Interpretation and scope] Under clause (ii) of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], $J\cdot E$ is the power density supplied to the matter model of that coupling, so the two identities read as a local, respectively fixed-volume, energy balance of the field and that matter model. Nothing is claimed for a prescribed current without such a matter model, for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular sources, or at field points where the products defining $u$ or $S$ are not locally integrable; the fixed-volume identity retains its boundary term and asserts no conservation unless that term vanishes or is included in the chosen system. The theorem is a conditional consequence of the adopted postulates and is not an empirical claim.
before.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct componentwise computation for (a); the parameter-integral lemma and the divergence theorem for (b). (a): the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], read componentwise) gives $\partial_tu=\varepsilon_0\langle E,\partial_tE\rangle+\mu_0^{-1}\langle B,\partial_tB\rangle$ with the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Substituting Faraday's law $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and the Ampere-Maxwell law in the form $\mu_0^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B=\varepsilon_0\partial_tE+J$ (using $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ from [[def-em-si-conventions]]) gives
$$\partial_tu=\mu_0^{-1}\bigl(\langle E,\operatorname{curl}B\rangle-\langle B,\operatorname{curl}E\rangle\bigr)-E\cdot J=-\mu_0^{-1}\operatorname{div}(E\times B)-J\cdot E,$$
where the last step is the cross-product divergence identity $\operatorname{div}(E\times B)=\langle\operatorname{curl}E,B\rangle-\langle E,\operatorname{curl}B\rangle$ of [[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]]; since $S=\mu_0^{-1}E\times B$, this is the asserted display. (b): fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and choose $t_0<t_0'<t<t_1'<t_1$. The maps $u$ and $\partial_tu$ are continuous on the compact set $\overline{\Omega'}\times[t_0',t_1']$, so [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] applied to the compact measurable $\overline{\Omega'}$ permits differentiation under the integral sign; then [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], whose hypotheses (finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation, $C^1$ field on the closure, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) are met by $S$ on $\Omega'$, converts $\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S$ into the boundary flux; $J\cdot E$ is continuous and hence integrable on $\overline{\Omega'}$. Clause (c) records the interpretation under [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] and the exclusions of the weak branch, singular sources and non-integrable products; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the divergence theorem, and no empirical premise is used.

before.title: Retarded potentials, Lorenz gauge and Maxwell fields of a compactly supported conserved smooth source
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the retarded-kernel and Cauchy suppliers below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the laboratory region, chart and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], so that $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. Let $a>0$, $t_0<T$ and let $ho:\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R	o\mathbb R$, $J:\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R	o\mathbb R^3$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] that are jointly of class $C^\infty$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], vanish identically outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)	imes[t_0,T]$, and satisfy the continuity equation $\partial_tho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ everywhere -- the compatibility condition that [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] shows to be forced by the Maxwell system, here assumed for the prescribed source. Define the retarded potentials by the explicit retarded integrals $$\varphi(x,t):= rac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3} rac{ho igl(y,t-|x-y|/c igr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):= rac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3} rac{J igl(y,t-|x-y|/c igr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and put $E:=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=
abla	imes A$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]). Then: (a) [Smoothness and wave equations] $\varphi$ and each component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, and $W\varphi=ho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise. (b) [Lorenz gauge] With $G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ one has $G=0$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: the retarded pair is in Lorenz gauge, and this is exactly where the continuity hypothesis is used. (c) [Maxwell fields] $E$ and $B$ are of class $C^\infty$ and the tuple $(E,B,ho,J)$ satisfies the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the whole of $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: $\operatorname{div}E=ho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $
abla	imes E=-\partial_tB$, $
abla	imes B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. (d) [No field before the source] $E=B=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$ (indeed $\varphi=A=0$ there): the selected retarded solution carries no field from before the source acted. (e) [Zero-data Cauchy identification] For every $t_1<t_0$ the pair $(\varphi,A)$ restricted to $\mathbb R^3	imes[t_1,\infty)$ is the unique $C^2$ extension solution of the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] at time $t_1$ with zero Cauchy data and sources $ho/\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0J$. (f) [Total charge] The total charge $Q(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}ho(y,t)\,dy$ is zero for every $t$: a source that is smooth, compactly supported in space and restricted to a compact time interval and satisfies continuity carries zero total charge, so this branch does not model an eternal isolated nonzero charge. (g) [Scope] This is the compact smooth branch with an adopted causal selection; it asserts nothing about point, line or sheet sources, about weak or distributional branches, about finite-energy or decay properties, about radiation reaction or self-force, and no empirical claim. In particular the fields of a prescribed isolated point charge with an eternal worldline are not covered by this theorem and are supplied separately by the point-source items of this page.
before.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. (a) $ho,J$ are $C^\infty$ with compact support, hence $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R)$; clause (b) of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] applied to $h=ho/\varepsilon_0$ and componentwise to $h=\mu_0J_k$ states that $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)dy$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ and satisfies $W(K*h)=h$ pointwise, which is exactly the display. Note the identification $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*ho$, $A=\mu_0K*J$ is the framework's form of the adopted retarded selection of [[post-em-radiation-selection]]; the selected branch is the object being computed, not assumed to exist a priori. (b) Differentiate the explicit retarded integral. In the substitution $y'=x-y$, which leaves the integral unchanged by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]), the kernel $1/(4\pi|y'|)$ is independent of $x$, so differentiating under the integral sign in $x$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]], applicable because the integrand is smooth and compactly supported in $y$ for $(x,t)$ in a bounded set) gives $\partial_{x^i}(K*h)=K*(\partial_{y^i}h)$; differentiating in $t$ gives $\partial_t(K*h)=K*(\partial_th)$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}A=\mu_0K*(\operatorname{div}J)$ and $c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*(\partial_tho)=\mu_0K*(\partial_tho)$ because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0\cdot\varepsilon_0^{-1}c^{-2}$ reduces to $\mu_0$ (equivalently $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$, [[def-em-si-conventions]]). Adding, $G=\mu_0K*(\partial_tho+\operatorname{div}J)=0$ by the assumed continuity. (c) $\varphi,A$ are $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, and clause (a) of [[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] (instantiated at $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$) states the exact identities $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG$ and $
abla	imes B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+
abla G$; with (a) and (b) these read $\operatorname{div}E=ho/\varepsilon_0$ and $
abla	imes B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J$. The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $
abla	imes E+\partial_tB=0$ are automatic for a potential pair by the curl-divergence and curl-gradient cancellation recorded in clause (c) of the same item and [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. This is the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. (d) If $t<t_0$ then for every $y$ the retarded argument satisfies $t-|x-y|/c\le t<t_0$, where $ho$ and $J$ vanish; both integrands vanish identically, so $\varphi(x,t)=A(x,t)=0$ and hence $E=B=0$ at such events. (e) Fix $t_1<t_0$. By (d), $\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$ and $\partial_t\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, and likewise for $A$; by (a) the pair is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes[t_1,\infty)$ and solves the sourced wave equations there. Clause (b) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] (uniqueness for $C^2$ extension solutions of the Cauchy problem with these data) identifies the pair with its zero-data solution; clause (d) of the same theorem gives the corresponding finite-speed support, consistent with (d). (f) $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_tho(y,t)dy=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=0$: for a ball $B_R$ with $R>a$ the divergence theorem ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]) converts the integral of $\operatorname{div}J$ into a boundary flux where $J=0$, and differentiation under the integral sign is licensed by compact support ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); hence $Q$ is constant, and $Q(t)=0$ for $t<t_0$ by (d), so $Q\equiv0$. (g) records the branch boundaries. No self-force, no product of distributions and no empirical premise is used; the only choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, inherited from the kernel and Cauchy suppliers through the surface-measure and convergence interfaces cited inside them.
before.physical_scope: Retarded potentials and fields of a prescribed smooth conserved source of compact spatial support in a compact time interval, on the whole laboratory spacetime in the framework's inertial chart: Lorenz gauge, the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations, zero field before the source acts, the zero-data Cauchy identification and zero total charge. Excluded: point, line, sheet or non-integrable sources; weak/distributional branches; eternal isolated charges; finite-energy, decay or boundary claims; self-force and radiation reaction; and every empirical or measurement claim.

used_after.title: Retarded potentials, Lorenz gauge and Maxwell fields of a compactly supported conserved smooth source
used_after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the retarded-kernel and Cauchy suppliers below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the laboratory region, chart and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], so that $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. Let $a>0$, $t_0<T$ and let $ho:\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R	o\mathbb R$, $J:\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R	o\mathbb R^3$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] that are jointly of class $C^\infty$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], vanish identically outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)	imes[t_0,T]$, and satisfy the continuity equation $\partial_tho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ everywhere -- the compatibility condition that [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] shows to be forced by the Maxwell system, here assumed for the prescribed source. Define the retarded potentials by the explicit retarded integrals $$\varphi(x,t):= rac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3} rac{ho igl(y,t-|x-y|/c igr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):= rac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3} rac{J igl(y,t-|x-y|/c igr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and put $E:=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=
abla	imes A$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]). Then: (a) [Smoothness and wave equations] $\varphi$ and each component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, and $W\varphi=ho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise. (b) [Lorenz gauge] With $G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ one has $G=0$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: the retarded pair is in Lorenz gauge, and this is exactly where the continuity hypothesis is used. (c) [Maxwell fields] $E$ and $B$ are of class $C^\infty$ and the tuple $(E,B,ho,J)$ satisfies the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the whole of $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: $\operatorname{div}E=ho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $
abla	imes E=-\partial_tB$, $
abla	imes B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. (d) [No field before the source] $E=B=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$ (indeed $\varphi=A=0$ there): the selected retarded solution carries no field from before the source acted. (e) [Zero-data Cauchy identification] For every $t_1<t_0$ the pair $(\varphi,A)$ restricted to $\mathbb R^3	imes[t_1,\infty)$ is the unique $C^2$ extension solution of the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] at time $t_1$ with zero Cauchy data and sources $ho/\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0J$. (f) [Total charge] The total charge $Q(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}ho(y,t)\,dy$ is zero for every $t$: a source that is smooth, compactly supported in space and restricted to a compact time interval and satisfies continuity carries zero total charge, so this branch does not model an eternal isolated nonzero charge. (g) [Scope] This is the compact smooth branch with an adopted causal selection; it asserts nothing about point, line or sheet sources, about weak or distributional branches, about finite-energy or decay properties, about radiation reaction or self-force, and no empirical claim. In particular the fields of a prescribed isolated point charge with an eternal worldline are not covered by this theorem and are supplied separately by the point-source items of this page.
used_after.strategy:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. (a) $ho,J$ are $C^\infty$ with compact support, hence $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R)$; clause (b) of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] applied to $h=ho/\varepsilon_0$ and componentwise to $h=\mu_0J_k$ states that $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)dy$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ and satisfies $W(K*h)=h$ pointwise, which is exactly the display. Note the identification $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*ho$, $A=\mu_0K*J$ is the framework's form of the adopted retarded selection of [[post-em-radiation-selection]]; the selected branch is the object being computed, not assumed to exist a priori. (b) Differentiate the explicit retarded integral. In the substitution $y'=x-y$, which leaves the integral unchanged by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]), the kernel $1/(4\pi|y'|)$ is independent of $x$, so differentiating under the integral sign in $x$ (direct dominated difference quotients: on each compact (x,t) parameter neighborhood all derivatives of h(x-y',t-|y'|/c) vanish outside one bounded y'-ball and are bounded by their appropriate derivative suprema; each quotient is dominated by that constant times |y'|^-1, integrable by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives each derivative identity. The smooth nonsingular [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] is used separately for the charge integral, not at this pole) gives $\partial_{x^i}(K*h)=K*(\partial_{y^i}h)$; differentiating in $t$ gives $\partial_t(K*h)=K*(\partial_th)$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}A=\mu_0K*(\operatorname{div}J)$ and $c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*(\partial_tho)=\mu_0K*(\partial_tho)$ because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0\cdot\varepsilon_0^{-1}c^{-2}$ reduces to $\mu_0$ (equivalently $\mu_0c^2\varepsilon_0=1$, [[def-em-si-conventions]]). Adding, $G=\mu_0K*(\partial_tho+\operatorname{div}J)=0$ by the assumed continuity. (c) $\varphi,A$ are $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, and clause (a) of [[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] (instantiated at $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$) states the exact identities $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG$ and $
abla	imes B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+
abla G$; with (a) and (b) these read $\operatorname{div}E=ho/\varepsilon_0$ and $
abla	imes B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J$. The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $
abla	imes E+\partial_tB=0$ are automatic for a potential pair by the curl-divergence and curl-gradient cancellation recorded in clause (c) of the same item and [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. This is the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. (d) If $t<t_0$ then for every $y$ the retarded argument satisfies $t-|x-y|/c\le t<t_0$, where $ho$ and $J$ vanish; both integrands vanish identically, so $\varphi(x,t)=A(x,t)=0$ and hence $E=B=0$ at such events. (e) Fix $t_1<t_0$. By (d), $\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$ and $\partial_t\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, and likewise for $A$; by (a) the pair is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes[t_1,\infty)$ and solves the sourced wave equations there. Clause (b) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] (uniqueness for $C^2$ extension solutions of the Cauchy problem with these data) identifies the pair with its zero-data solution; clause (d) of the same theorem gives the corresponding finite-speed support, consistent with (d). (f) $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\partial_tho(y,t)dy=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=0$: for a ball $B_R$ with $R>a$ the divergence theorem ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]) converts the integral of $\operatorname{div}J$ into a boundary flux where $J=0$, and differentiation under the integral sign is licensed by compact support ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); hence $Q$ is constant, and $Q(t)=0$ for $t<t_0$ by (d), so $Q\equiv0$. (g) records the branch boundaries. No self-force, no product of distributions and no empirical premise is used; the only choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, inherited from the kernel and Cauchy suppliers through the surface-measure and convergence interfaces cited inside them.
used_after.physical_scope: Retarded potentials and fields of a prescribed smooth conserved source of compact spatial support in a compact time interval, on the whole laboratory spacetime in the framework's inertial chart: Lorenz gauge, the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations, zero field before the source acts, the zero-data Cauchy identification and zero total charge. Excluded: point, line, sheet or non-integrable sources; weak/distributional branches; eternal isolated charges; finite-energy, decay or boundary claims; self-force and radiation reaction; and every empirical or measurement claim.

before.title: Causal convolution response, transfer function and dispersion relations
before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#D1-D2 (compact and W^{1,1} integrable causal branches), assembled with the passivity quadratic form
before.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the smooth Riemann/Lebesgue comparison route below; in clause (c), also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) inherited from the AC supplier. Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. For any $b>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, the full entire-plane bound is $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}\prime\prime\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$. Its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous entrywise in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$, with $K\prime$ its almost-everywhere derivative with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and apply the relations to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
before.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). On $[0,b]$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts]] twice to the real and imaginary parts of the smooth exponential and real smooth kernel (first $K$, then $K\prime$). All derivatives are continuous and Riemann integrable; [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]] transfers each compact-interval identity to the Lebesgue integrals. With vanishing endpoint values because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and beyond $b$, these identities give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated upper-half-plane $|z|^{-2}$ bound; for arbitrary complex $z$, $|e^{izs}|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on the support gives the full entire-plane bound. For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|\chi_{jk}|/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; its explicit AC definition and Lebesgue FTC/integration-by-parts route apply entrywise under the inherited Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; its boundary contour uses vertical shifts before passing to the real boundary.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian dissipative part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). On $[0,b]$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts]] twice to the real and imaginary parts of the smooth exponential and real smooth kernel (first $K$, then $K\prime$). All derivatives are continuous and Riemann integrable; [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]] transfers each compact-interval identity to the Lebesgue integrals. With vanishing endpoint values because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and beyond $b$, these identities give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated upper-half-plane $|z|^{-2}$ bound; for arbitrary complex $z$, $|e^{izs}|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on the support gives the full entire-plane bound. For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|\chi_{jk}|/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; its explicit AC definition and Lebesgue FTC/integration-by-parts route apply entrywise under the inherited Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; its boundary contour uses vertical shifts before passing to the real boundary.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian dissipative part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

before.title: Uniform far-zone asymptotics and retarded-time flux limit for compact conserved smooth sources
before.statement:
Let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$ and $t_0<T$ be constants, let $\rho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ and $\mathbf J\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy (H1) $\rho(y,v)=\mathbf J(y,v)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ or $v\notin[t_0,T]$, and (H2) $\partial_v\rho+\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. For $x$ with $r:=|x|\ge2a$ define the retarded scalar and vector potentials $$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad \mathbf A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and the fields $\mathbf E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$, $\mathbf B:=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, where the derivatives are taken in $x$ and all objects are read on $\{|x|\ge2a\}$.

(a) (Fields as retarded integrals.) On the open set $\{|x|>2a\}$ the potentials $\varphi,\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ in $(x,t)$, and there $$\mathbf E(x,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf N}{R^2}c^2\rho\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)+\frac{\mathbf N}{cR}c\,\rho_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)-\frac{\mathbf J_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)}{R}\Bigr]dy,$$$$\mathbf B(x,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf N\times\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-\frac Rc)}{R^2}+\frac{\mathbf J_t(y,t-\frac Rc)}{cR}\Bigr]dy,$$ where $R:=|x-y|$, $\mathbf N:=(x-y)/R$, and $\rho_t,\mathbf J_t$ are the partial derivatives in the second variable. Moreover, on $\{|x|\ge2a\}\times[t_0,T]$, $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ coincide with the corresponding solution constructed in the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and scalar source $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$, respectively $h=\mu_0 J_k$.

(b) (Uniform far-zone expansion.) For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$ put $\mathbf I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and $\mathbf V(n,u):=\partial_u\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$. Then $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\frac1c\,n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$, and there are constants $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$, depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and on the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, such that for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$, with $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V(n,u))$, $$\Bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \Bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

(c) (Retarded-time flux limit.) Let $\mathbf S:=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and let $d\Omega$ be the surface measure on $S^2$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then for every $u\in[t_0,T]$, $$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}\bigl|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)\bigr|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$ This is a limit at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time $t$; no decay or boundary condition at spatial infinity is assumed beyond the compact spatial support in (H1).
before.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, with explicit uniform estimates; the polar-coordinate identity uses the wave Cauchy problem as the definition of the retarded solution.

(a) On $\{|x|>2a\}$ one has $|x-y|\ge a>0$ for $y\in\overline B_a$, so the integrands of $\varphi$ and $\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ jointly in $(x,t,y)$ on a neighbourhood of $\{|x|>2a\}\times\mathbb R\times\overline B_a$; differentiating under the integral over the compact set $\overline B_a$ in each parameter direction ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]) and using the chain rule for $(x,t)\mapsto(y,t-|x-y|/c)$ gives $\nabla_x[f(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N[f/R^2+f_t/(cR)]$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J/R^2+\mathbf J_t/(cR)]$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); substituting into $\mathbf E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ gives the displayed field integrals and the smoothness claim. The identification with the wave Cauchy problem is the polar-coordinates identity: by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], applied to $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$ and to each component $h=\mu_0J_k$ (to the positive and negative parts, then subtracted), $$\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\int_0^\infty r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr,\qquad M_rh(x,v)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,v)\,d\sigma(n);$$ substituting $r=c(t-v)$ in the $r$-integral with the one-dimensional $L^1$ change-of-variables formula for the $C^1$ diffeomorphism $v\mapsto c(t-v)$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]], applied on the compact interval where the continuous integrand is bounded) turns the right-hand side into $c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h(\cdot,v)(x)\,dv$ for $t\in[t_0,T]$, which is exactly the function displayed in clause (a) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and source $h$.

(b) Elementary bounds in the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]): for $|y|\le a$ and $r\ge2a$ one has $R^2-(r-n\cdot y)^2=|y|^2-(n\cdot y)^2$ with $R+(r-n\cdot y)\ge r$, hence $|R-(r-n\cdot y)|\le a^2/r$, $|\mathbf N-n|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r-a)\le5a/r$ and $|1/R-1/r|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r(r-a))\le2a/r^2$, uniformly in $n,y$. Consequently $t-R/c=u+n\cdot y/c+O(a^2/(rc))$ uniformly, and comparing the field integrals of (a) with the candidate leading terms, each correction term (the $\rho/R^2$-term, the $\mathbf N-n$, $1/R-1/r$ and retarded-argument corrections) is bounded by an explicit constant times $r^{-2}$, the constants involving only $a,c,\mu_0$ and the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on the compact set $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$ (mean value theorem in the time variable; [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The surviving terms of order $r^{-1}$ are $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}\bigl[c\,n\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy-\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy\bigr]$, the second integral being $\mathbf V(n,u)$ and the first computed from the continuity equation: applying the divergence theorem for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], with $\Omega$ a ball of radius $R>a$ containing the spatial support, whose boundary flux vanishes because $\mathbf J$ vanishes off $B_a$) to $y\mapsto\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ gives $0=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}_y[\mathbf J(\cdot,u+n\cdot y/c)]=\int_{\mathbb R^3}[\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J+\frac nc\cdot\mathbf J_t](y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); by (H2) and continuity of $\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J$, this is $\int\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy=\frac1c n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$. Substituting, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[c\,n\,\frac1c(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[n(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V)$ by the vector triple-product identity, and the leading term of $\mathbf B$ is $-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}n\times\mathbf V=\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}}{c}$, so the stated uniform errors follow with the constants just described.

(c) From the leading fields, $n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=0$ and $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{lead}}=\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times(n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=(|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n-(n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n/c$, while $|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times(n\times\mathbf V)|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times\mathbf V|$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Hence $r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2+R(n,u,r)$ with $|R|\le C/r$ uniformly in $n,u$ for an explicit $C$ obtained from $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$. The sphere is compact of finite surface measure, the map $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] gives smoothness of $\mathbf I$, hence of $\mathbf V$, in $n$), and uniform convergence of the integrands gives the displayed limit without any further limit/integration exchange ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention used by that definition is declared in the item contract, [[def-countable-choice]]).

The surviving terms of order $r^{-1}$ are $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}\bigl[c\,n\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy-\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy\bigr]$, the second integral being $\mathbf V(n,u)$ and the first computed from the continuity equation: applying the divergence theorem for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], with $\Omega$ a ball of radius $R>a$ containing the spatial support, whose boundary flux vanishes because $\mathbf J$ vanishes off $B_a$) to $y\mapsto\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ gives $0=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}_y[\mathbf J(\cdot,u+n\cdot y/c)]=\int_{\mathbb R^3}[\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J+\frac nc\cdot\mathbf J_t](y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); by (H2) and continuity of $\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J$, this is $\int\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy=\frac1c n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$. Substituting, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[c\,n\,\frac1c(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[n(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V)$ by the vector triple-product identity, and the leading term of $\mathbf B$ is $-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}n\times\mathbf V=\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}}{c}$, so the stated uniform errors follow with the constants just described.

(c) From the leading fields, $n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=0$ and $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{lead}}=\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times(n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=(|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n-(n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n/c$, while $|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times(n\times\mathbf V)|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times\mathbf V|$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Hence $r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2+R(n,u,r)$ with $|R|\le C/r$ uniformly in $n,u$ for an explicit $C$ obtained from $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$. The sphere is compact of finite surface measure, the map $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] gives smoothness of $\mathbf I$, hence of $\mathbf V$, in $n$), and uniform convergence of the integrands gives the displayed limit without any further limit/integration exchange ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention used by that definition is declared in the item contract, [[def-countable-choice]]).
 Scalar normalization check for (a): phi=mu0 c²/(4pi) integral rho(y,t-R/c)/R, so -grad phi=mu0/(4pi) integral [c²N rho/R²+c N rho_t/R]; subtracting A_t adds -mu0 J_t/(4pi R). The second electric term has one factor c, consistent with (b)'s c n integral rho_t and epsilon0^-1=mu0 c².

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, Cambridge lecture notes (236-page author-hosted PDF)
references.locator: Sections6.4.1–6.4.3 printed158–164 supply the potential/field background. The additional proper-history distributional wave/gauge and C1 cutoff proof is explicit here against exact library suppliers; no distributional point-source theorem is attributed to this text.

used_after.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let c>0, epsilon0>0, q in R, mu0=(epsilon0 c²)^-1, and let z:R->R³ be C³ with |z'(s)|<=v*<c for all s. These are mathematical parameters. On Q=R³ times R let rho,J and Phi,Upsilon be exactly the proper point-current and retarded-history distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] and [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], with the kernel K of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and no independent free addition. Put W=c^-2 partial_t²-Delta. Then (a)
$$W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad W\Upsilon=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(Q).$$
(b) Define the vector distributions $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$ and $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$ using componentwise [[def-distributional-derivative]] and the usual finite-coordinate cross/curl convention [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. They satisfy
$$\operatorname{div}\mathcal E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\quad\operatorname{div}\mathcal B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}\mathcal E=-\partial_t\mathcal B,\quad\operatorname{curl}\mathcal B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_t\mathcal E.$$
(c) On the complement of Gamma={(z(s),s)}, these distributions restrict to the exact C1 Lienard-Wiechert fields of the earlier point-potential lemma, with all its higher-regularity branches retained. The zero extensions of those E,B formulas on Gamma belong to L1loc(Q), and their regular distributions are precisely mathcal E,mathcal B ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). The off-worldline C1 fields also satisfy the source-free classical Maxwell equations there, because the point pair restricts to zero and each continuous regular residual is zero. Thus the equations in (b) are equations for locally integrable fields with the exact point source, not merely arbitrary field distributions. No field value on Gamma is physically assigned; zero extension is a representative convention on a null set. No physical adoption, nonlinear distribution product, finite self-energy, self-force, global acceleration bound, or incoming-field uniqueness theorem is asserted.
used_after.strategy:
Use only the existing explicit histories, not an undefined convolution of two noncompact distributions. Fix psi in D(Q) with observation support |x|<=M,t0<=t<=t1. The earlier point-potential proof gives a common proper-history cylinder [-S,t1] times B_L for every contributing (s,y), where S=max(0,(M+|z(0)|-ct0)/(c-v*)) and L=1+M+|z(0)|+v*max(S,|t1|); derivatives of psi have the same observation support. All relevant absolute integrals are bounded by a derivative supremum times integral over that cylinder of 1/|y|, finite by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], with the actual nonnegative order rules [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. If the history interval is empty all pairings vanish.
For F(y,s)=(K circledast psi)(y,s), each parameter derivative is K circledast the corresponding test derivative. Indeed on a bounded parameter neighborhood, the spatial projection of psi's support confines the kernel variable to one bounded ball; every difference quotient is dominated by its test-derivative supremum times |w|^-1 there. Dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] and the scalar FTC show F is smooth and give those identities for all derivatives. For each fixed (y,s), translation of WK=delta from [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] yields (K circledast Wpsi)(y,s)=psi(y,s). Apply this pointwise identity inside the bounded absolute history integrals: <Phi,Wpsi>=q/epsilon0 integral psi(z(s),s)ds and <Upsilon_j,Wpsi>=mu0 q integral z'_j(s)psi(z(s),s)ds, proving the two distributional wave equations, including q0.
The function s->F(z(s),s) is C1 by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and has compact support in the same finite history interval: cone causality gives the upper bound, uniform subluminality gives the lower bound. Its derivative is F_s+z' dot grad_y F. Therefore the distributional Lorenz residual tested on the ORIGINAL SMOOTH psi equals
$$-\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}[z'(s)\cdot\nabla_yF(z(s),s)+F_s(z(s),s)]ds=0,$$
by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], using c^-2/epsilon0=mu0. No derivative or cutoff is moved onto a noncompact distribution test. By [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]], finite coordinate cancellations give div curl0,curl grad0 and curl curl Upsilon=grad div Upsilon-Delta Upsilon. With G=div Upsilon+c^-2 Phi_t, direct algebra gives div mathcal E=W Phi-G_t and curl mathcal B-c^-2 mathcal E_t=W Upsilon+grad G. The two wave identities and G0 prove all four equations.
Locality and local integrability. A continuous regular distribution vanishing on an open set has its function identically zero: injectivity of [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] gives zero almost everywhere, and a nonzero continuous value would give a nonzero neighborhood of positive measure by [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]. Thus classical derivative compatibility below also yields the four source-free classical equations off Gamma. The earlier lemma supplies regular Phi,Upsilon and C2 potentials on Q minus Gamma. Its C1 field formulas and the classical-compatibility clause of the distributional differentiation theorem give the stated restrictions. The graph is closed and null: each fixed-time spatial section is a singleton. The Borel graph is product-measurable by [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], and [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] identifies product and Euclidean measure under the declared Countable Choice; hence Tonelli [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] gives zero four-dimensional measure. On any compact observation cylinder Q0, retarded s lies in [-S,t1], so A_Q=max_{[-S,t1]}|z''| is finite. With b*=v*/c, kappa>=1-b*, the explicit fields obey |E|+|B|<=C_Q(r^-2+r^-1), with constants depending on |q|,c,epsilon0,b*,A_Q, not on the individual observation point. The earlier C1 diffeomorphism g(s,y)=(z(s)+y,s+|y|/c) has absolute Jacobian kappa<=1+b*. The earlier proof establishes its global diffeomorphism property; the exact [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]], under the declared Countable Choice, gives
$$\int_{Q_0}r^{-p}dxdt\le(1+b_*)(t_1+S)_+\int_{B_L}|y|^{-p}dy<\infty\qquad(p=1,2).$$
The last integrals are 4pi L²/2 and 4pi L respectively. Thus zero-extended classical E,B are L1loc; this alone is not yet identification across Gamma.
No hidden curve delta in the first potential derivatives. Put d=|x-z(t)|. Since t-s=r/c and |z(t)-z(s)|<=b*r, one has (1-b*)r<=d<=(1+b*)r. Potentials are consequently bounded by C/d on each compact observation cylinder. Choose a smooth spatial cutoff chi on R³, zero on B1 and one outside B2, with bounded derivative ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]); set chi_epsilon(x,t)=chi((x-z(t))/epsilon). This is C3, sufficient for CLASSICAL C1 integration by parts, but it need not be a C-infinity distribution test. Its spatial gradients are bounded by C/epsilon, its time derivative by Cv*/epsilon, and all are supported on epsilon<=d<=2epsilon. Ordinary compact C1 products with the original psi can be integrated by parts in each coordinate via [[thm-integration-by-parts]], followed by finite rectangle Fubini and [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] under the declared Countable Choice; equivalently extend chi_epsilon times each potential by zero, which is C1 across its vanished neighborhood. For any first spatial or time derivative D, the resulting ordinary integral identity is
$$\int \chi_\epsilon(Df)\psi=-\int \chi_\epsilon f D\psi-\int f(D\chi_\epsilon)\psi,$$
where f is any potential component off Gamma. On the cutoff shell |f|<=C/epsilon, |Dchi_epsilon|<=C'/epsilon. Spatial translations give shell volume O(epsilon³) at each t ([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]), and the time interval of psi is fixed; the last integral is O(epsilon). Since f and its classical first derivatives are L1loc (the latter also follow directly from the earlier D-gradient and D_t formulas with bounded compact-history acceleration), dominated convergence lets epsilon tend0 in the first two integrals. It gives -integral f Dpsi=integral (Df)psi for each ORIGINAL smooth psi. Hence global distributional first derivatives have exactly the locally integrable classical representatives, and their finite combinations identify mathcal E,mathcal B with zero-extended E,B. No product of distributions, singular-field value, stronger worldline regularity, or noncompact test action enters.

before.title: Complete retarded point fields: unique retarded root, the delta substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$, Liénard-Wiechert potentials and fields, and a uniform far-zone remainder
before.design_state: complete-exact-declared-branch-conditional-research-argument; direct dependency list reconciled with the actual proof uses and the root clause stated in event form (batch-22 notes)
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

(b) [Delta substitution and Liénard-Wiechert potentials] Let $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the point-source distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] attached to $q$ and the worldline $z$, let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ and define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=(q/\varepsilon_0)\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, componentwise in the second case. These are the history-integral interpretation supplied by clause(b) of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], not ordinary distribution action on a noncompact test. Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions to $\Gamma$ of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. The uniformity is in the direction $n$ at a fixed emission event $s_0$; no uniformity in $s_0$ is asserted ($z''$ is not assumed bounded), and no finite-energy, decay or radiation-flux conclusion is drawn.

This is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved, and the uniform speed bound and the exclusion of $\Gamma$ are essential hypotheses (see the companion example page).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

(b) [Delta substitution and Liénard-Wiechert potentials] Let $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the point-source distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] attached to $q$ and the worldline $z$, let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ and define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=(q/\varepsilon_0)\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, componentwise in the second case. These are the history-integral interpretation supplied by clause(b) of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], not ordinary distribution action on a noncompact test. Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions to $\Gamma$ of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. The uniformity is in the direction $n$ at a fixed emission event $s_0$; no uniformity in $s_0$ is asserted ($z''$ is not assumed bounded), and no finite-energy, decay or radiation-flux conclusion is drawn.

This is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved, and the uniform speed bound and the exclusion of $\Gamma$ are essential hypotheses (see the companion example page).
